text:
## The short version

**Qi2** and **Qi2.2** are open standards from the Wireless Power Consortium. **MagSafe** is Apple's own branding and implementation, and Apple's current charger is certified to the newest Qi standard.

| | Qi2 | Qi2.2 (Qi2 25W) | MagSafe |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who owns it | Wireless Power Consortium (WPC) | WPC | Apple |
| Max power | 15W | 25W | 15W for most iPhones, up to 25W on newer ones |
| Magnets | Yes, magnetic ring | Yes | Yes |

**Qi2** added a magnetic ring to Qi, which aligns the phone and charger for faster, more efficient charging. Apple contributed MagSafe technology to it. It's capped at 15W. ([The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/news/708060/qi-2-2-certification-25w-wpc-belkin-anker-ugreen-aukey))

**Qi2.2** is the same idea at 25W. The WPC says that's nearly 70% more power, and about 0 to 50% in roughly 30 minutes. The WPC brands it "Qi2 25W," so you may see either name. The first certified products appeared in July 2025. ([WPC](https://www.wirelesspowerconsortium.com/standards/qi-wireless-charging/))

**MagSafe** is Apple's version. Apple-certified MagSafe accessories deliver 15W to most iPhones and up to 25W to the newest ones. According to Macworld, certified chargers also include an NFC antenna so the iPhone can identify them, and a magnetometer to prevent compass interference. Cheap "MagSafe-compatible" chargers are usually just magnets with 7.5W charging. ([Macworld](https://www.macworld.com/article/668980/best-magsafe-chargers.html))

## What your phone can actually use

- **iPhone 12 through 15, and 17e:** up to 15W. Qi2 and MagSafe chargers perform about the same.
- **iPhone 16 and later:** 25W is possible, but it varies by model. Apple lists up to 25W for the iPhone 17 series and the 16 Plus and 16 Pro Max, 22.5W for the iPhone 16 and 16 Pro, and 20W for the iPhone Air. You need a 30W or greater adapter. ([Apple Support](https://support.apple.com/en-ie/105047))
- **Android:** support is thin. The Pixel 10 Pro XL supports Qi2.2 at 25W, other Pixel 10 models support 15W, and Samsung's Galaxy lineup is "Qi2 Ready," meaning it needs a magnetic case. ([The Verge](https://www.theverge.com/gadgets/939362/best-magsafe-qi2-2-batteries-power-banks))

Everything is backward compatible, so a 25W charger works fine with a 15W phone at that phone's speed.

## If you're buying

- **Apple MagSafe Charger** is certified for Qi2 25W and works with any Qi2 phone. The 2 m version is $49 at [Apple](https://www.apple.com/shop/product/mgdm4ll/a/magsafe-charger-2-m?fnode=7120d2e211c5d2008372acfadfa9b649c5ec92879b07e2f040e38952fcd8be0794ade18a93d927b4c96c7a13cda2597927c0814a65dc0189e774b77c7fdb7e748fe7efe26c0c6c21f59929ac37012aa0ac916746c2f56a8e6448ccdb97e7d384&fs=s%3Dnewest%26fh%3D8e12f5%252B81eaf8). Macworld lists the 1 m at $39.
- **Baseus PicoGo AM52 Qi2.2 power bank** (10,000 mAh) was the fastest wireless charger in The Verge's test. It took an iPhone 17 Pro Max to 65% in an hour. Code `AM52` takes $6 off, to $53.99, via [this link](https://dealectric.com/go/baseus-picogo-am52-qi2-2-10000mah-45w). That's an affiliate link to Baseus's store, and the code was last tested 2026-10-25, so confirm at checkout.

To check that a charger is really certified, you can search the WPC's product database.
